title: Quench-wave latency scratchpad
body:
Context: quick scratchpad for a weird ingress pattern I kept seeing in staging: very short, high-intensity surges (50-200ms window) repeated every ~10s, with long idle between waves. I'm calling it 'quench-wave' because bursts then apparent cooldown. Goal: reproduce and measure tail latency and validate that KV-prefix priming + tiny-batching keeps p99 reasonable without sacrificing throughput.

Test harness:
- Load generator: envoy-ratelimit-proxy + custom spike-driver (node)
- Target: hosted-like instance (dedicated small pool) running xformer-gpt-6B-quant (4-bit quant), variant v2026-02-14
- Hardware: 1xA100-80GB (dedicated test node), CUDA 12.2 drivers
- Runtime flags: continuous-batching enabled, max_batch_ms=6, prefer_kv_cache=true, eager_prefill=false
- Sequence length: prompt 32 tokens + gen up to 64
- Concurrency pattern: baseline steady qps 10, quench-wave: 800 qps for 120ms (spike window), repeat every 10s for 10 cycles
- Measurement: p50/p95/p99, 95th CPU util, GPU SM utilization, GC pauses, request success rate, lost-connections

Priming variants:
A) cold (no priming), B) prefix-prime 10 synthetic requests 128-context (writes to KV cache), C) dynamic-mini-batching (client packs 2 small reqs into single batch), D) prefix-prime + dynamic-mini-batching + soft-throttle (client-side adaptive backoff)

Raw results (mean across 5 runs, 10 cycles each):
scenario,p50_ms,p95_ms,p99_ms,throughput_qps,success_rate,gpu_sm_pct,cpu_pct
cold,12,98,372,220,0.997,83,28
prefix-prime,10,84,210,215,0.999,78,24
mini-batch,11,76,166,275,0.998,89,31
prime+pack,9,72,138,290,0.999,86,29
prime+pack+throttle,12,92,132,250,1.00,68,21

Notes on the table: throughput_qps is aggregate offered throughput sustained during spikes (not steady-state). Cold run p99 spikes to ~372ms — large tail. Packing helps because it increases per-batch tokens processed efficiency (improved throughput) but raises SM utilization; success_rate dips slightly when we push to 290 qps in mini-batch cases. The soft-throttle variant keeps success at 1.00 and reduces GPU pressure but costs some throughput.

Telemetry snapshots (selected interesting cycles):
- Cycle 3 (cold): sudden queue depth spike -> worker-side queue grew to 320, queue-timeouts 4, GC pauses visible ~18ms due to allocator churn.
- Cycle 5 (prime+pack): KV-hit rate jumped to 0.86 immediately after priming, average request saw 1.6x fewer KV misses, tail reduced ~40%.

Quick ascii timing diagram (conceptual):
[idle..............][spike 120ms][cooldown 9.88s][spike][...]
Within spike: many requests arrive within 30ms front-loaded, trailing sub-window of small requests. If prefix didn't exist, first 30ms incurred KV fetch + warmup penalties.

Observations / hypotheses: 
- KV prefix priming materially reduces p99 in this pattern — confirms that key cache misses during the first wave front are a dominant tail contributor.
- Mini-batching/packing increases throughput and reduces kernel startup overhead, but raises instantaneous GPU utilization and risks connection failures if we do no backoff.
- Soft-client-side adaptive throttle (detect short-term SM >85%) prevents saturation-induced timeouts and improves success (useful tradeoff for customer-facing SLAs).
- Eager_prefill=false seems fine for throughput but if we toggle eager_prefill=true (server-side pre-alloc of KV slots) we might reduce first-wave p99 further — add as next check.

Questions to follow up: 
- Does increasing max_batch_ms to 10 (trade latency for larger batch) reduce p99 without hurting p50? Need a quick sweep.
- What is the cost delta (token-cost) when we prefix-prime vs cold for a real workload (i.e., extra synthetic tokens per minute)? rough calc: 10 primes * (128 tokens) * cycles/min -> need cost estimate.
- If we enable eager_prefill on the serving runtime, what's incremental memory overhead and eviction behavior with 100 tenants?

Action items / next runs: 
- Run A/B with max_batch_ms=6 vs 10 for prime+pack+throttle scenario (short sweep). owner: Ozzie. target date: next week.
- Add eager_prefill=true single-node test with small eviction window and monitor kv-eviction / miss rates. owner: Lea.
- Instrument client to record instantaneous enqueue delay histograms (already added minimal hooks; expand to 1ms bins). owner: Mika.

Notes to self: stash the driver config used for prime+pack+throttle run under /tmp/quench-ozzie/ for reproducibility. Also post short summary to #perf with the CSV and the three takeaways (priming, packing, soft-throttle).

Quick summary (2 lines): Quench-wave pattern causes big first-wave p99s via KV misses and kernel startup overhead. Best immediate mitigation is cheap: prefix priming + lightweight packing + adaptive client throttle — good SLA/throughput sweet spot.

Raw artifacts: test runner config: https://gist.github.com/ozzie/quench-runner-2026 (private), telemetry dump: s3://redwood-perf/quench/ozzie/2026-03-09.tar.gz

End of scratch.
